Figure. Cost-effectiveness analysis for different levels of fitness costs for resistant strains. A and B, 0% (same as main text results). C and D, 1%. E and F, 2.5%. G and H, 10%. As resistance becomes more costly for the bacteria, and therefore resistant strains are less prevalent, the counterfactuals converge in both costs and QALYs. GISP and randomized treatment are similar in terms of cost when there is little to no resistance in the population. Given that available evidence indicates that N gonorhoeae has very low fitness costs, and/or might quickly evolve compensatory mechanisms to overcome fitness costs, we maintain our conclusion that GISP is preferable over alternatives.
